This is my first post and I searched a little bit to check and see if this question had already been asked, but I didn't find anything that similar, so here's my question.

I'm an undergraduate doing summer holography research at my university and one thing we're trying is true color holography. We've done some test exposures with a yellow Tweetie wrapped in red wire (we only have a green and a red laser at the moment, we're waiting on the blue) and we noticed that at certain angles, he'll be all green, all yellow, or all red. We don't get any differentiation between the yellow Tweetie and the red wire. 

I guess that's my question, as well as why he's different colors at different reference beam angles.

Our setup includes a red HeNe laser at 633 nm, a green HeNe laser at 543 nm and a soon to be purchased tunable Argon laser. The beams are combined with dichroic filters, intensities are adjusted with variable neutral density filters in front of each laser, and each beam passes through the same apochromatic microscope objective and 50 micron pinhole. The beam expanding from the spatial filter setup (at this moment) is yellow and is incident on a glass plate holder, behind which lies our object.

posts.author: Kaveh
posts.content_md:
Sounds like you have a good source of equipment, so use it to get some great results!!

The biggest problem in wavelength choice is the improper choice of green, which gives you bad yellows. Your 543 is near the optimum of 540, so I would expect very good yellows. 

OK, so you are making single beam Denisyuk holograms of a Tweetie in a red wire. (I had to look up Tweetie in Wikipedia, so now I know it is yellow!)

First of all, let's make sure that your choice of wavelengths is not distorting colors. What do you see when you forget holograms, and just illuminate the object with the composite yellow beam? Do you see the correct colors? Any angle dependence?

If the objects look good in that light, then your wavelengths are good from a color rendering viewpoint, and the problem is the holographic recording.

I have a feeling that you are only recording a hologram with one of the wavelengths, and the different colors you see are while you tilt the plate in white light. 

Is your recording material suitable for both wavelengths? Few are...

Have you tried making two exposures, one with green, one with red? That's the first thing to try. 

Making color holograms is not easy, and attention to detail is essential. 

You might find some details in my thesis on holography useful:

[http://www.focalimage.com/public/kaveh-PhD.pdf](http://www.focalimage.com/public/kaveh-PhD.pdf)

Happy to answer any more queries. You can also email me offline:

kaveh at river-valley.com

posts.author: Kaveh
posts.content_md:
First of all, do you see the object more or less in the correct colors, when you illuminate with the yellow (red+green) light with no other light around? 

What you are doing is superimposing two hologram made with two wavelengths. To get the original colors, you need to make sure your emulsion is not shrinking, so if you make a green recording, then using white light to reconstruct show you the image in green.

So the Green light will reflect well off the Tweetie, but not the red wire. On the other hand the red will reflect off both well. These will add together in the right proportions to give you the correct colours.

I strongly suggest you do not complicate things by adding the blue laser till you know what is going on with the two colors. Blue is usually the more difficult too.

posts.author: Hans
posts.content_md:
I think that the hologram should not re-play in pure light of a yellow wavelength. However, if the yellow re-play light is a combination of red+green and thus looks yellow to the eye (but is not really yellow), it should play back the yellow image.

Yes, the hologram is a combination of a red and a green hologram. You could even expose the plate in red and green in separate exposures. But I don't know if that is advantageous to the final result.

What you should check is that the colours of your tweety reflect both the red and the green beam. JohnFP has done extensive research into this with several paint colours and their reflectivity with respect to different wavelength. In short: A yellow subject might not look yellow when illuminated by a red and green laser at the same time because your yellow might not reflect one of those primary colours at all.

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
Yes, what Kaveh stated and Hans reinforced is you may have alackofcolor (sorry I couldn't resist). BTW, welcome to the forum!!!

Let me try to explain further what Kaveh mentioned twice. Take the Tweetie and look at it in the red laser light alone, not the hologram but the object. The Tweetie should look Red and the wire should look Red. Now look at the Tweetie in the Green light. The Tweetie should now look green and the wire should look black. Is this the case?

Also, as I mentioned, most "wire" is coated with a shiny outer coating. If this is the case the the reflection of red light off the wire may be acting as a mirror reflection and missing the plate completely or only hitting it at one point, not diffusely hitting the entire plate.

May I suggest you change or paint your object such that you have the following colors on your object, it may help you a lot.

A Red that looks red at 633 and looks black at 543

A Green that looks black at 633 and green at 543

A Yellow that looks red at 633 and looks green at 543.

You can take another object that is rigid and just paint three differenct sections to these three colors. (HINT: look at the paints in the laser light before using). I have found that what looks like red in ordinary light may also reflect 543 and thusly will reflect both wavelengths resulting in a yellowish color. Most paints have white in them so even though a bright red looks red it will reflect other wavelengths as well.

Finally, I stress, you have to make sure you processing is correct by making a hologram of a green object only with the green laser and insure it is green after processing. Then maintain this as your standard processing.

posts.author: Ed Wesly
posts.content_md:
Sounds like you need to calibrate your materials. Try to make a series of exposures of the subject with each laser individually. The exposure series should be logarithmic; i.e. since you think lower exposures look brighter, expose for 500 microJ, 1 mJ, 2 mJ, and maybe even 4 mJ. Keep your processing times constant. Do it for both lasers.

Once you see what is the brightest for each wavelength, cut the exposure dose in half for each and try both lasers on a single plate. Then you can play with balancing them to get the best color rendition.

How much power do you have with your Gre-Ne? I think the biggest I ever saw was a 5 mW from Melles Griot! Is it polarized?

Good luck and keep us posted.

posts.author: Hans
posts.content_md:
> We are still noticing color changes depending on the incident angle of white light. We made one with just the red laser today and noticed that it looks green at shallow reconstruction angles, yellow at less shallow ones, and red when it's near the reference beam angle. Can someone explain this to me? Thanks

This is normal behaviour of a hologram. If you look up this link: [http://www.eserc.stonybrook.edu/ProjectJava/Bragg/](http://www.eserc.stonybrook.edu/ProjectJava/Bragg/), it will become clear why this is so. Imagine the interference planes in your hologram as being thin mirrors that are all spaced apart approximately half the wavelength of your laser. When you shine white light at the original angle to your hologram, only the red component of the white light will be able to be reflected back to you because only the red light from all the parallel reflection interference mirrors will interfere constructively. All the other wavelengths will interfere destructively with reflection from the deeper interference planes (mirrors) or not at all.

Now, when you change the angle of the white light that illuminates the plate, the distance that the light travels between the parallel reflection planes is different. This allows light a different to interfere constructively.

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md:
If it was homemade, does it have external mirrors? If so you can inset a bewsters plate and polarize it and maintain most of the power. If the mirrors are inside the tube you are stuck.

I like the C315-100mw 532nm laser. See Laser Types in the wiki.

However if you are doing three seperate exposures then you could set up the Ar+ laser for 514nm.

posts.author: Hans
posts.content_md: You could also just hang a simple polarizing sheet in front of the laser. But as the direction of polarisation might not fluctuate in a constant and predictable manner, it will be difficult to determine the correct exposure time as it will be different for each exposure.

I got mine from Mr. Gizmos. They are all takouts from lithography machines (I believe the industry went to blue). They are used and in a variety of conditions. The Mr. Gizmos ones are tested and adjusted by Laser Sam himself. I paid about $1500 for mine and it cam with a bunch of optics that I promtply packaged and boxed up and never used. If you can get the Head and controller that is all that is useful. I had to supply it with a low noise voltage source but I had an old switching supply that worked just fine.

The beam is beautiful, it has a little more divergence than I would have expected but that is not very important for holography until you have three colinear beams. The coherence length is extremely long. The beam is circular and guasian. 

It is a ring design but there is a very small second line that has not been of importance to holographers. This laser is revolutionizing holography.
